w: Valparaiso runs sixteen funiculars up its hills, but only one is a true elevator rather than a slope-climbing car: the Polanco Lift rises vertically through a shaft tunneled into the rock. Three stations connect Simpson Street to Polanco Hill. These days tourists ride it more than the locals it was built to serve.

Like most of the ascensores, it survives as everyday transport for hill residents as much as a novelty for visitors passing through.

It passed out of private hands in 1971, reopening as a fine arts museum, and was declared a Chilean historic monument in 1976 -- one of the grandest surviving houses from Valparaiso's boom-era elite.

w: Before 1825, non-Catholics who died in Valparaiso were buried on Playa Ancha hill or thrown into the sea. British consul George Seymour bought land by the city jail to found this Protestant cemetery instead. Its roughly 800 graves, mostly British, German and American, include a monument to sailors from USS Essex, captured in 1814.
_facts: founded 1825 for Protestant and non-Catholic burials

w: El Peral was Valparaiso's first funicular built with steam traction, and its chimney became the line's signature feature. It links Plaza de la Justicia with Paseo Yugoslavo, a clifftop walk over the bay. The upper station still lets riders see the old propulsion machinery that hauled the cars.

w: Merchant Benigno Polanco Humeres built this mansion in 1903 on reclaimed land in El Almendral, once lined with grand palaces from Valparaiso's boom era. The 1906 earthquake destroyed every other one; only this survived. Carabineros have used it since 1942; restoration begun in 2016 followed damage from the 2010 quake.

The old Intendencia building on its far side now houses the Chilean Navy's headquarters.

w: Founded in 1873 with the Chilean government's blessing, this was the country's first public library and still holds 80,000 volumes. Its current building, raised between 1912 and 1919, was damaged in the 2010 earthquake and later restored -- long after it was declared a National Monument, back in 1998.
